In the commission-with-fees-passed scenario, the attendees pay the $89,000 in fees (on top of face value), while the organizer keeps the full $1,000,000 face revenue. In the commission-absorbed scenario, the festival covers those fees and fans pay exactly face value – meaning the organizer nets $911,000. In the flat fee scenario, fans also pay face value, and the organizer nets around $970,000 after costs (assuming ~$30k total cost, which in this example works out to about 3% per ticket). This simple example shows how a flat model can drastically reduce costs if you have high volume – but it also assumes the organizer had the funds to pay that flat fee and manage only receiving $97 instead of $100 per ticket. Every festival’s numbers will differ, so plug in your own and compare. Festival Ticketing Fees: Absorbing vs. Passing on to Attendees Beyond the pricing model, one strategic decision every festival producer faces is what to do with ticketing fees – absorb them into your ticket price or pass them along to the buyer as extra charges. This is a crucial consideration in how your event is perceived and how much revenue you actually pocket. Let’s break down the trade-offs: Exploring Strategic Revenue-Share Partnerships — How large-scale organizers turn ticketing fees into a shared revenue stream for the event. Passing Fees On – “Plus Fees” Pricing Most large ticketing platforms allow you to pass their service fees and processing charges directly to the customer. You advertise a base ticket price, and at checkout, the buyer sees something like “+$X service fee + $Y order processing”. The benefit to you as the organizer is clear: you get the full face value of the ticket (minus any taxes) and the ticketing company collects its fees from the attendee. Your advertised price is lower, which can make the event seem more affordable at first glance, and your budget forecasts are simpler because a $50 ticket earns you $50. However, the downside is potential sticker shock and customer frustration . Many fans feel nickel-and-dimed by add-on fees. They might select a $50 ticket, see a total of $63 after fees and taxes, and then bail on the purchase. In fact, hidden fees revealed at checkout are a primary reason people abandon ticket purchases. Public sentiment has increasingly turned against excessive ticket fees – a 2024 UK study found that fees added about 18% on average to concert ticket face values , and in some cases markups reached 30–40% when all charges were included . Those sorts of headlines amplify fan anger. If your festival’s audience is particularly fee-sensitive (for instance, a community festival or an all-ages event where parents buy multiple tickets), passing high fees on could damage your reputation. Recover Lost Ticket Sales Automated abandoned cart emails re-engage potential buyers at the optimal time, recovering lost sales and boosting your conversion rate. Abandoned Cart Recovery for Events Get Started Free It’s worth noting that regulators and big players are reacting to this issue. Live Nation (parent of Ticketmaster) recently implemented all-in pricing at its festivals and venues – showing customers the full price upfront – after finding that fans responded positively to transparency. They expected some conversion drop, but were surprised and thrilled to find no reduction in sales when they led with final prices; in fact, consumers loved seeing the final price from the start. This suggests that even if fees are ultimately paid by the customer, being honest about them is key. If you do pass on fees, consider displaying an “all-in” price early (e.g. on your website: “Tickets $108.90 including fees”) to avoid nasty surprises at checkout. Absorbing Fees – “Fees Included” Pricing Absorbing fees means the price you advertise already includes the ticketing costs – the attendee pays one round number, and you, the organizer, will pay the ticketing provider out of that. For example, if you set your ticket at $55 including fees and the platform’s fee is $5, you’ll net $50. The obvious drawback is you, not the buyer, bear the cost – your revenue per ticket is lower. However, there are some compelling advantages to this approach: – Transparent pricing builds trust: Fans see a flat $55 and know exactly what they are paying. As veteran promoters often note, a fair pricing reputation yields long-term dividends . You’re signaling that you’re not trying to slip in extra charges. This can boost conversion rates; some attendees who would balk at a $50+fees ticket might be perfectly fine with a $55 “no additional fees” ticket. Psychologically, it feels more fair. – Simpler marketing message: It’s easier to market “Tickets $55 (all fees included)” on posters and social media. You eliminate the asterisk and fine print about fees. Some festivals even make “no fees” a selling point in their promotions, distinguishing them from other events. This was a strategy embraced by certain UK festivals after seeing widespread fan frustration with hidden fees – they raised the face value a bit but promised no surprises at checkout, earning goodwill. – Competitive advantage: If all your competitors or other events in your genre are tacking on 15% in fees, including fees in your price can make your total cost to attend lower or on par, even if your face value looks slightly higher. In areas or countries where consumers are especially cost-conscious (or where regulations require upfront pricing), absorbing fees can set you apart. (For instance, New Zealand and Australia have consumer laws encouraging upfront disclosure of mandatory fees.) Uncovering Hidden Platform Expenses — Identifying the total cost of ownership beyond the initial advertised per-ticket rate. Of course, absorbing fees does cut into your margins. You need to account for it in your budget. Many festivals solve this by simply raising the base ticket price enough to cover the average fee. It requires forecasting your average fee per ticket (which might vary by ticket type or price). If it’s a percentage, the math is straightforward: for a 5% fee, increase prices by ~5.3% to cover it (so that after 5% is taken, you’re left with your target amount – essentially dividing target price by 0.95). For mixed percentage + fixed fees, you aim to cover the average case. It might not be perfect down to the cent, but you can get very close. One risk to watch with fee-inclusive pricing: taxes . Depending on your locale, absorbing fees might mean you’re paying sales tax on the full ticket price including what will later go to the ticketing service. When fees are passed on, in some regions those fees aren’t taxed as your revenue. Consult with an accountant – the difference is usually marginal, but it’s worth noting if you’re operating in a tight budget or dealing with VAT/GST on tickets. The Best of Both Worlds? Some festivals try a hybrid approach. For example, you might include most fees in the ticket price but still add a small order or shipping fee at checkout (especially if physical wristband shipping is involved). Or you absorb the base platform fee but pass on credit card fees as a “payment processing surcharge” of a few percent, since many consumers are accustomed to that on various bills. This can keep your advertised price close to reality while still offloading a bit of cost. If you do this, be very transparent about it (“Ticket includes all fees except a 3% payment processing charge”). The last thing you want is to regain trust by including fees, then lose it by sneaking in another surcharge. So which to choose – pass on or absorb? It depends on your pricing strategy and brand positioning. If your festival markets itself on fan-friendliness or you’re in a competitive market where every dollar counts, consider absorbing or at least being upfront about fees. As one expert festival ticketing guide put it, a reputation for fairness is worth far more in the long run than a bit of extra fee revenue today. On the other hand, if margins are razor-thin and you simply cannot afford to eat the fees, pass them on but try to keep them reasonable. Some platforms allow you to split fees – e.g., you cover the fixed $1 portion but pass the percentage to fans, so both sides share the burden. And remember, whichever route you go, communicate it clearly to avoid confusion. Sometimes a platform with a higher fee can actually deliver better net revenue to your festival by boosting sales or reducing other costs. Conversely, a low-fee platform might end up costing you more in missed opportunities or operational headaches. Here are some key trade-offs and features to evaluate , based on decades of festival production experience: Mastering High-Pressure Gate Operations — Ensuring a seamless entry experience with reliable hardware and expert on-site technical support. Marketing Tools and Sales Boosters One of the biggest hidden impacts on your bottom line is how well a ticketing platform helps you sell tickets . This goes beyond fees and into features. For example, built-in marketing tools like referral programs can dramatically increase your sales without extra ad spend. Industry veterans note that referrals (attendees recruiting their friends) are often the highest-ROI marketing channel. Data from real festivals shows that integrating a referral program into ticketing can drive 15–25% higher ticket sales on average . That’s a huge boost – and if those extra tickets wouldn’t have sold otherwise, it’s essentially extra revenue at no cost aside from small referral rewards. Consider a scenario: Platform A charges 2% per ticket with no marketing features. Platform B charges 5% but includes a robust refer-a-friend system and loyalty incentives. If Platform B’s tools lead to even 10% more tickets sold (due to fans promoting the event), the additional revenue likely outweighs the 3% fee difference. In fact, some festivals have reported 20:1 ROI on referral incentives – meaning for every $1 worth of free drink or discount given as a referral reward, they got $20 in ticket sales . Those are trade-offs to consider. When comparing costs, ask: What am I getting in return for this fee? Higher fees that come with powerful marketing integrations, analytics, or audience reach might deliver better net results. Other sales boosters include social sharing discounts, urgency timers, abandoned cart remarketing, and promo codes . If a platform helps you capture abandoned purchases (for example, by emailing those who didn’t complete checkout – something Ticket Fairy’s system can automate), you might recover a sizable chunk of otherwise lost sales. Even event discovery features – being listed in a major ticketing site’s marketplace – can drive additional ticket buyers you wouldn’t have reached on your own. These benefits are harder to quantify, but they matter. A platform with a huge built-in audience might justify a higher service fee if it brings you hundreds of extra customers for free. On the flip side, if you already have a loyal fan base and do your own marketing, paying extra for a platform just because it has a big directory (full of other events) might not be worth it. Always align platform strengths with your festival’s specific needs. Data Ownership and CRM Value In 2026 and beyond, data is gold for festival organizers . The ability to own and use your attendee data can directly affect your bottom line through repeat sales and sponsorships. Some ticketing companies essentially “rent” you the ticket buyers but keep the customer relationship for themselves – they might restrict full access to emails or require that any marketing to attendees goes through their system (sometimes for an additional cost). This is a hidden cost: if you can’t easily reach your audience for next year’s festival, you’ll spend more on advertising or lose out on returning attendees. Securing Your Attendee Data Goldmine — Why owning your customer relationships reduces future marketing spend and boosts sponsorship value. Choosing a platform with full data ownership means you get all buyer info and can export it into your CRM or email marketing tools. For example, Ticket Fairy provides 100% data access (every email, buyer demographic, etc.), empowering organizers to re-engage fans directly . The long-term value of this is immense. Imagine telling a prospective sponsor you have 50,000 verified email addresses of attendees with opt-in data on music preferences – that could increase your sponsorship deal value. Or consider that marketing to your past ticket buyers via email and social lookalike audiences is far cheaper than acquiring new cold audiences. Over a few years, the festivals that control their data will spend less on marketing and see higher retention. When comparing platforms, ask if they allow you to own the customer relationship . If a lower-fee platform limits your data access or monetizes your attendees with other offers, that might cost you more in the end. As one 2026 festival industry report put it, data ownership is not just a tech concern but a financial one – it directly ties into your event’s growth and revenue potential. Payout Schedules and Cash Flow Another often-overlooked factor is when you get your ticket revenue disbursed . Different ticketing platforms have different payout schedules: some pay you as tickets are sold (daily or weekly settlements) , while others hold funds until after the event. This can hugely impact your cash flow. For example, if you sell $1 million in tickets but your provider holds that until after the festival, you need to finance all your pre-event expenses another way (loans, credit, etc.). That financing has a cost – interest payments or opportunity cost of tied-up capital. Platforms that offer frequent payouts or even advance payout programs provide a financial edge. Ticket Fairy, for instance, has a program called TICKETFAIRY Capital that can advance organizers a portion of projected ticket sales (often ranging from $10,000 up to seven figures) to cover upfront costs like artist deposits and production expenses. These advances are recouped from ticket sales, with no exorbitant interest like a bank loan. If your festival is in growth mode, this kind of feature protects you from cash crunches. It effectively lowers your financial risk, which is a huge trade-off to consider alongside pure fee percentages. An advance might save your event if you’re short on initial funds for critical deposits. Optimizing Pre-Event Cash Flow — How frequent payout schedules provide the liquidity needed to pay artist deposits and vendor invoices on time. Even without formal advance programs, simply getting paid as you go can save thousands in credit costs. A real-world example: an Australian New Year’s festival cited that switching to a provider with weekly payouts allowed them to pay staging and staffing invoices on time without short-term loans. The money they saved on interest and late fees outweighed the slightly higher ticketing fee they were paying compared to their old platform. In contrast, some budget ticketing services that hold funds until after the event have indirectly caused festivals to fold – the organizers ran out of cash before show day. In summary, when evaluating cost, consider the time value of money . If one platform charges 2% and holds your cash, and another charges 3% but pays you immediately, the latter might be the safer choice if you need liquidity. Cash flow is the lifeblood of festival production, and ticketing is often the main source of that cash. Anti-Fraud, Security, and Scalping Prevention Fraud and scalping can introduce both financial and reputational costs. If a platform has poor fraud prevention, you might eat chargeback costs for fraudulent transactions (some providers even charge you a fee for each chargeback). Additionally, rampant scalping can drive up secondary prices, angering fans who might blame the festival. Modern fan-first ticketing platforms put measures in place to combat these issues. Tools like anti-bot protections, ticket purchase limits, and face-value resale marketplaces help ensure real fans get tickets at the intended price . Why is this in a cost comparison? Because a platform that allows unchecked scalping might hurt your long-term attendance – fans priced out by bots this year might not even try next year. Or, if your event develops a reputation for fake tickets circulating, you may need to invest more in customer support and on-site security to remedy it. A provider like Ticket Fairy includes a secure resale marketplace where ticket holders can only resell to other fans at face value, with the new buyer’s ticket getting reissued seamlessly. This not only cuts out scalpers (protecting your community and brand), but also keeps money in the ecosystem – a happy fan who can resell a ticket they can’t use is more likely to buy again next time. Eliminating Scalping and Ticket Fraud — Protecting your community and brand reputation with secure, face-value resale marketplaces. While it’s hard to put a dollar value on this, think of it as an insurance policy. You might be willing to pay a slightly higher fee for a platform known for robust fraud prevention if it avoids a disaster like 500 counterfeit tickets showing up at your gate or a social media firestorm about $500 resales on a $100 ticket. Some festivals have learned the hard way via viral news stories that fan trust is priceless – and they’ve since switched to ticketing solutions that prioritize security and fairness . Customer Support and On-Site Operations Finally, consider the “soft” costs of using the platform: your team’s time and the risk of things going wrong. An intuitive system with good support might save you countless hours (which in a festival crunch time is literally money). Does the platform help you easily solve issues like ticket transfers, VIP credentialing, or scanning offline in a rural field with spotty Wi-Fi? These operational capabilities can prevent costly delays at entry or angry customers at the box office demanding refunds. For instance, if a ticketing platform provides on-site personnel or a dedicated support line during your event , you can resolve scanning glitches or database issues in minutes, avoiding long lines. Some festivals pay extra for this service if it’s not included – which is fine, but include it in your cost comparison. The peace of mind from knowing your entry system won’t crash (and if it does, someone is there to fix it immediately) is worth paying for. Conversely, saving 1% in fees by using a no-frills platform is not worth it if it leaves you stranded on show day. One way to gauge this is to look at case studies or ask other festival organizers about their experiences. If a platform helped a festival handle a sudden 10,000-person surge at gates smoothly, that’s a good sign. Reliability and support often distinguish the truly professional platforms from the hobby projects. As a veteran producer will tell you, the fee you pay is also for the “service” part of a ticketing service. Make sure you’re getting service that matches your festival’s needs. Sometimes industry-leading uptime and support are explicitly part of the pitch – for example, systems boasting 99.9% uptime and proven performance under high traffic . Don’t ignore those aspects in your cost calculus. A ticketing outage during an on-sale could mean thousands in lost revenue if fans give up or bad PR if they rage online about queue issues. Making an Informed Decision When comparing ticketing platform costs, festival organizers should approach it like any major investment – weigh the total cost of ownership against the total benefits delivered . Here’s a quick recap of how to evaluate your options: Map out all fees: Create a spreadsheet for each platform you’re considering. Include per-ticket fees, credit card processing, any monthly subscription or minimum, setup fees, payout fees, refund fees, etc. This comprehensive view prevents surprises. (If a provider isn’t transparent about a fee category, ask directly.) Remember the advice: understand all fees and how they affect pricing , including “hidden” ones like equipment rental or extra service charges. Run scenarios: Use your best-case and worst-case ticket sales projections to calculate what you’d pay under each platform’s model. Also plug in a middle scenario. This will show you at what attendance level each option becomes expensive or advantageous. Identify your breakeven points for commission vs. flat as discussed earlier. Consider who pays the fees: Decide on your stance about passing fees to attendees vs. absorbing. If one platform’s fees are too high to comfortably pass on (e.g., would make your checkout price unappealing), that’s a red flag. You might lean towards a solution with fan-friendly pricing that keeps add-ons reasonable. Keep in mind the long-term fan relationship; short-term gains from hefty fees can lead to long-term losses in loyalty . Many top festivals now choose providers that prioritize fair pricing to avoid alienating their audience. Factor in feature value: Make a list of the features that matter for your festival and note which platform offers them (and at what cost). If one includes a powerful referral marketing program, integrated RFID wristband support, or a robust analytics dashboard , that could save you money you’d otherwise spend on third-party tools or extra staff. For each feature, ask “Does this save me money or increase revenue?” If yes, that platform’s higher fee might be justified. For example, full data ownership might not have an obvious dollar value today, but next year when you’re selling 70% of your tickets to last year’s attendees via direct email (because you had their contacts), you’ll see the payoff. Assess support and reliability: Try to quantify the importance of reliability for you. If a cheaper platform has any history of outages or poor support, consider the potential cost of a ticketing failure. Sometimes it’s worth paying a premium for peace of mind. As the saying goes, “you get what you pay for.” An anecdote from a festival organizer: after a nightmare with a bargain ticketing app that crashed during the on-sale (causing furious emails and lost sales), they opted to switch to a more established platform mid-cycle. They effectively paid fees twice that year (once to each platform) – an expensive lesson that reliability and capacity should have been part of the comparison. Look at the fine print: This includes refund policies (especially after the pandemic, know whether the platform will refund their fees to attendees if the event cancels, or if you’ll be eating those fees), contract terms (any exclusivity or multi-year commitments?), and integration costs (APIs, scanners, payment processors – are they included or do you need separate accounts?). A “low cost” platform that doesn’t refund fees on canceled events, for example, could cost you hundreds of thousands if a catastrophe strikes and you choose to refund fans to maintain goodwill. After doing this homework, you’ll likely find one or two providers that stand out as the best fit. At this point, it’s absolutely worth having a direct conversation with those platform’s reps. Ask for a detailed cost breakdown based on your event’s specifics. Reputable ticketing partners will be happy to provide a transparent quote and even advice on the best fee configuration (pass on vs include, etc.) based on their experience with similar festivals. Unlocking Viral Fan-Led Growth — Turning your attendees into a marketing force that offsets platform costs through increased sales volume. Finally, don’t be afraid to negotiate – especially if you’re a large event or have unique circumstances. Many platforms have flexibility on rates, or can throw in value-adds (like on-site staffing, custom development, or marketing support) if they want your business. Use the data you’ve gathered: if one platform is clearly cheaper in your analysis, you can leverage that when talking to another provider (“Platform X is offering a 2% fee with weekly payouts – can you match that, or can you offer something extra that justifies the difference?”). The ticketing market is competitive in 2026, and as a festival organizer you have more choices than ever, from giant international firms to niche indie platforms. Conclusion and Next Steps Comparing ticketing platform costs might not be the most glamorous part of festival planning, but it’s one of the most important for safeguarding your event’s revenue. The right choice means more money stays in your festival, helping you deliver a better experience for fans and a healthier profit for your team. The wrong choice can siphon off tens of thousands in fees or stunt your marketing efforts – truly the lifeblood of a growing festival. Remember that “best value” doesn’t always mean “lowest fee.” It means the platform that optimally balances cost with features, support, and growth potential for your festival. A transparent fee structure that aligns with your scale, a toolset that boosts your sales, and a partner that won’t let you down when it counts – those are the things to look for. As one festival producer wisely put it, focus on what you keep, not just what you pay . If a platform helps you sell more tickets or saves you headaches, that’s money in the bank. If you’re ready to explore a modern, festival-focused ticketing solution further, consider checking out a specialized festival ticketing platform built for multi-day events that offers transparent pricing and robust features. Many leading festivals have found success by switching to fan-first ticketing systems that put attendees first and eliminate surprise fees. The Ticket Fairy platform, for example, has no dynamic pricing (so fans always pay the advertised price), and it provides extras like referral marketing, face-value resale, and real-time analytics as part of its package. Ultimately, the decision is yours – and it should be an informed one. Use the comparisons and calculations we’ve discussed to protect your festival’s revenue . We’re happy to walk you through exact cost projections and show how our tools can boost your ticket sales while keeping costs fair. Thank you for reading this guide. By demystifying ticketing platform costs, we hope you feel empowered to make the best choice for your festival and your fans. Frequently Asked Questions What are the main pricing models for event ticketing platforms? Most event ticketing platforms use either a per-ticket commission model or a flat-rate subscription structure. Commission models charge a percentage plus a fixed fee per ticket sold, while flat-rate models charge a predictable monthly or annual fee regardless of sales volume. Both typically add separate payment processing fees. How much do ticketing platforms charge for per-ticket service fees? Ticketing platforms typically charge a commission between 2% and 5% plus a fixed $0.50 to $2.00 per ticket. For example, Eventbrite charges organizers approximately 3.5% plus $1.59 per ticket. These service fees usually exclude credit card processing charges, which add another 2.5% to 3% per transaction. How do you calculate the break-even point for ticketing platform costs? Calculate the break-even point by dividing a flat-rate platform’s total subscription cost by the per-ticket commission fee of a pay-as-you-go platform. For example, a $1,500 flat fee divided by a $2.50 per-ticket commission equals 600 tickets. Selling more than 600 tickets makes the flat-fee model more cost-effective. Should festival organizers absorb ticketing fees or pass them to attendees? Festival organizers must choose between absorbing fees to build fan trust or passing them on to preserve profit margins. Passing fees on maintains face-value revenue but risks cart abandonment from sticker shock. Absorbing fees requires raising base ticket prices by approximately 5% to cover platform costs while offering transparent pricing. How do built-in referral programs offset festival ticketing fees? Built-in referral programs offset ticketing fees by driving 15% to 25% higher average ticket sales without additional advertising spend. Festivals utilizing these marketing tools often see a 20-to-1 return on investment, generating enough extra revenue through fan-to-fan promotion to easily justify a platform’s higher per-ticket commission rate. What hidden costs should event organizers look for in ticketing contracts? Event organizers should watch for hidden ticketing costs including separate credit card processing rates, upfront setup charges, and fees for exceeding flat-rate ticket caps. Additional unexpected expenses often include chargeback penalties, equipment rentals for on-site scanning, and premium charges for dedicated customer support or advanced marketing features. Why is attendee data ownership important for festival producers? Attendee data ownership allows festival producers to export buyer information directly into their CRM and email marketing tools. Controlling this data significantly reduces future advertising costs by enabling direct re-engagement with past buyers and increases overall event valuation when negotiating with potential festival sponsors. How do ticketing platform payout schedules impact festival cash flow? Ticketing platform payout schedules dictate when organizers receive their revenue, heavily impacting pre-event cash flow. Platforms offering daily or weekly settlements allow producers to pay staging and artist deposits without securing high-interest loans. Conversely, platforms holding funds until after the event force organizers to finance upfront production expenses independently.

body_text: Kornit Digital Redefines Apparel Production for the On-Demand Era Unveiling Atlas MATRIX at Konnections 2026 April 12, 2026 PDF Version For The First Time, Producers Operate With Complete Flexibility Across Cotton, Polyester, and Blended Fabrics, Printing What They Need, When They Need I t At The Highest Retail Quality Unified, Streamlined Production Significantly Reduces Production Complexity and Labor Requirements, Opens New Revenue Opportunities for Brands and Producers HOLLYWOOD, Fla., April 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Kornit Digital Ltd. (NASDAQ: KRNT, “Kornit Digital”, “Kornit”, or the “Company”), a global pioneer in sustainable, on-demand digital fashion and textile production, today unveiled its Atlas MATRIX at Konnections 2026, redefining apparel production in the on-demand era. Atlas MATRIX is the first unified digital production system designed to deliver true demand-driven manufacturing with complete flexibility across cotton, polyester, and blended fabrics, with no compromise on quality, durability, or efficiency. At its core is Kornit’s proprietary Karbon Shield technology, a breakthrough protection layer preventing dye migration even on the most challenging deep-dyed and sublimated polyester fabrics. Karbon Shield enables consistent, vibrant, and durable results in a true single-step process, without complex setups or manual intervention, while maintaining a soft hand feel that meets the highest retail standards. The system supports both direct printing using Karbon Shield and transfer on film using Karbon Transfer, ensuring full consistency between decoration methods and opening new possibilities for placement, design flexibility, and product categories. Atlas MATRIX also introduces expanded creative capabilities with two distinct configurations: a neon configuration designed for high-impact sports and performance applications, and a red and green configuration tailored for fashion and brand applications. “For years, the industry has been constrained by trade-offs, but that is finally changing,” said Ronen Samuel, Chief Executive Officer of Kornit Digital. “Screen printing can deliver strong results on polyester, but requires long setup times, multiple process steps, and additional costs to control dye migration and maintain consistency. Digital solutions, including earlier generations such as Atlas MAX POLY, did meaningfully expand the boundaries of what’s possible, yet performance on polyester depended on fabric type, process tuning, and operational complexity. Atlas MATRIX removes these limitations entirely, opens a massive market opportunity, and firmly positions digital as the new standard for apparel production.” Atlas MATRIX directly addresses one of the largest opportunities in the apparel industry by transforming how producers manage short- and mid-run jobs. Today, the global screen-printing market represents approximately 14 billion impressions annually, with nearly 6 billion impressions in run lengths below 1,000 units – segments where agility, speed, and flexibility are critical. Notably, about 30 percent of this volume includes polyester and blended materials, commonly used in fast-growing categories like sportswear and athleisure, which demand increasingly higher performance and quality standards. Atlas MATRIX is engineered to unlock this opportunity at scale. The impact goes beyond polyester, as Atlas MATRIX enables seamless production across cotton, blends, and performance fabrics in a single system, allowing producers to consolidate operations and enter new applications rapidly. Atlas MATRIX will be available for customer delivery starting early May, including upgrade packages for existing Atlas family systems such as Atlas MAX PLUS and Atlas MAX POLY. Customers can place orders immediately. In addition to its unveiling at Konnections 2026, Kornit will showcase Atlas MATRIX with live demonstrations at upcoming global industry events, including FESPA Global Print Expo in Barcelona, May 19–22, 2026. About Kornit Digital Kornit Digital (NASDAQ: KRNT) is a worldwide market leader in sustainable, on-demand, digital fashion and textile production technologies. The Company offers end-to-end solutions including digital printing systems, inks, consumables, software, and fulfillment services through its global fulfillment network. Headquartered in Israel with offices in the USA, Europe, and Asia Pacific, Kornit Digital serves customers in more than 100 countries. To learn more, visit www.kornit.com . body_text: Slay The Spire 2 is the direct sequel to the beloved Slay The Spire game, which was originally released back in 2019 and still bolsters an 'overwhelmingly positive' review score on Steam. The sequel has also introduced some brand new playable characters, and we're going to run over all of them below. Here's what we know. All Playable Characters In Slay The Spire 2 Slay The Spire has been one of the premier indie titles we've seen over the last couple of years, and with the rise in other indie games such as Mewgenics this year, we're amped for this one. Slay The Spire 2 will offer 5 playable characters at the time of it's release, and we can speculate that there will be more later down the line. The Ironclad Starting Relic: Burning Blood Starting Cards: Strike x5, Defend x4, Bash Starting Health: 80 The Silent Starting Relic: Ring of the Snake Starting Cards: Strike x5, Defend x5, Neutralize, Survivor Starting Health: 70 Unlock Conditions: Play as The Ironclad. The Regent Starting Relic: Divine Right Starting Cards: Strike x4, Defend x4, Falling Star, Venerate Starting Health: 75 Unlock Conditions: Play as the Silent. The Necrobinder Starting Relic: Bound Phylactery Starting Cards: Strike x4, Defend x4, Bodyguard, Unleash Starting Health: 66 Unlock Conditions: Play as the Regent The Defect Starting Relic: Cracked Core Starting Cards: Strike x4, Defend x4, Zap, Dualcast Starting Health: 75 Unlock Conditions: Play as the Necrobinder In the meantime, be sure to check out our Vulcan II TKL Pro , which is an exceptional choice for all titles.
